interactions.summary: Jiang explains the paradox that Virgil secretly helps create a Christian while remaining anti-Christian himself, then invites interpretations from the class.
Students propose empire and mercy as ways the Aeneid could drive someone toward Christ, and Jiang endorses the idea that the poem’s unresolved violence can make a reader seek a preacher.

claims.claim: Jiang says Statius treats wastefulness and greed as opposite extremes that collapse into the same moral structure.
Jiang calls it a paradox that Virgil could make Statius both a poet and a Christian even though Virgil himself is not Christian.
Jiang approves the reading that meditating on the Aeneid’s mercy-failure can make a reader search for Christ as the answer to what the poem lacks.
Jiang poses the unresolved problem that the same poem can convert everyone except its own author.

signature_moments.moment: The poem wounds a reader into looking for a preacher, which turns literary dissatisfaction into a road toward Christ.
signature_moments.source_phrase: made you look for a preacher
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang’s most compact account of how pagan epic can become Christian preparation.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil becomes the tragic exception: the work moves everybody except the one who wrote it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it can move everybody except virgil
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The line concentrates the whole father-poet paradox into one humiliating image.

chronology_notes.note: This packet records a June 26 formulation of Jiang’s theory that a text can contain a salvific pressure stronger than its author’s own explicit commitments.
